source.title_on_document: Generative AI Meets Open-Ended Survey Responses: Research Participant Use of AI and Homogenization

supplement.where: An 'Online Supplement' referred to in the text (PDF pp. 24, 26, 29, 30, 32, 33); no URL given in the preprint.
supplement.holds: Robustness results for GPT-4o mini at temperatures 0.0 and 1.0, GPT-4o, and Claude 3 Opus: Table S1 (length and vocabulary), Figure S1 (tf-idf terms), Figure S2 (sentiment), Figure S6 (pairwise cosine similarity), and other Moral Foundations dimensions.

paper_design_summary: Part I is a survey of 794 Prolific participants (summer 2024) on how often they use LLMs to answer open-ended survey questions, why, and how they would prompt an AI for three survey questions. Part II feeds the prompts of self-reported AI users to GPT-4o mini, Gemini 1.5, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet and compares the LLM answers with human answers to the same three questions from pre-ChatGPT TESS surveys (2019 to 2021), matched on demographics. The comparison scores length, vocabulary, distinctive words, sentiment, dehumanizing language, and average pairwise tf-idf cosine similarity within each source. No participant writes a scored answer with AI help.

studies.label: Part I: Prolific survey of self-reported LLM use on open-ended questions

participants.exclusions: 799 recruited; excluded 2 who did not consent, 2 who failed an attention check, and 1 flagged as a bot by a CAPTCHA (PDF p. 11 (10)).
participants.who: US adults on Prolific, recruited with Prolific's 'representative sample' quotas on ethnicity, gender, age, and political affiliation, summer 2024; 272 report using AI at least sometimes, 522 never (Table 3).
participants.quote: We recruited 799 participants to our study; our final analytic sample excludes two participants who did not give consent, two participants who did not pass an attention check
participants.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 10), Section 3.1; PDF p. 12 (11), Table 1 (N = 794)

ai_tool.name_model: None administered. Respondents report their own LLM use (ChatGPT used by over 90 percent of AI users; Gemini about 30 percent; Copilot about 22 percent).
ai_tool.how_used: Self-reported frequency of using 'AI assistants or chatbots' to answer open-ended survey questions; respondents also wrote the prompt they would give an AI for each of three TESS questions.

task.description: Survey questions on frequency of and reasons for LLM use, plus writing sample prompts for three open-ended TESS questions. Outcomes are self-reports, not scored output.

studies.label: Part II: LLM-simulated vs pre-ChatGPT human answers to three open-ended TESS questions

participants.exclusions: Prolific observations with no exact demographic match in TESS were pruned: 8 (JSD), 33 (Graham), 42 (Groenendyk) (PDF p. 26 (25)). LLM refusals and invalid outputs were dropped: 16 percent Claude 3.5 Sonnet, 14 percent Gemini 1.5, 1 percent GPT-4o mini (PDF p. 25 (24)).
participants.who: Corpus. Human answers from three TESS studies fielded on NORC's AmeriSpeak panel before November 30, 2022 (Jardina and Stephens-Dougan 'JSD', Graham, Groenendyk), each matched exactly on race/ethnicity, education, partisanship, and age group to one Prolific AI user's prompt; LLM answers generated from those prompts. Matched sets: n = 223 (JSD), 195 (Graham), 187 (Groenendyk).
participants.quote: At the end, we had matched sets of n = 223 for JSD, n = 195 for Graham, and n = 187 for Groenendyk. All analyses that follow are based on these matched sets.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4o mini (temperature 0.7), Gemini 1.5 (temperature 1), Claude 3.5 Sonnet (temperature 1) in the main analyses; GPT-4o, Claude 3 Opus, and other GPT-4o mini temperatures in the Online Supplement.
ai_tool.how_used: Researchers sent Prolific respondents' prompts to the models through the API and post-processed the outputs into survey-style answers; no person used the AI to write a scored answer.

task.description: Open-ended opinion survey answers: what comes to mind about [blacks | African Americans] in American society (JSD); what makes you similar to your party and different from the other (Graham); what makes you [uninterested | interested] in politics (Groenendyk).

outcomes.name: Average within-source pairwise cosine similarity of tf-idf vectors (homogeneity; higher = less diverse)
outcomes.question: none

contrasts.treatment_arm: LLM-generated answers (GPT-4o mini, Gemini 1.5, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, each separately)
contrasts.reported: Figure only (Figure 8, bars; no numbers printed in text or as bar labels). Text: 'for all three questions, the average pairwise cosine similarity between responses generated by the LLMs was higher than for responses generated by humans'; 'Responses from GPT-4o mini had the highest mean cosine similarities.' Higher similarity means less diverse, so the sign is reversed relative to the codebook. No standard error, confidence interval, or test is reported for this outcome in the preprint. The paper reports matched sets separately: n = 223 (JSD), n = 195 (Graham), and n = 187 (Groenendyk), on PDF p. 26 (printed p. 25), Section 5. These counts do not give the number of source-level sets or the final retained count for each model and question; n_units is null.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 33 (printed p. 32), Section 5.5, Figure 8; method on PDF p. 32 (31)

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity of response tf-idf vectors, used as a proxy for text homogeneity (PDF pp. 32-33, Section 5.5 and Figure 8).
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Not applicable: term frequency-inverse document frequency (tf-idf) vectors; no pretrained embedding model is used for this outcome.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Pairs of responses within each text source (human, GPT-4o mini, Gemini 1.5, or Claude 3.5 Sonnet), calculated separately for each TESS question (Graham, Groenendyk, and JSD).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No standard error, confidence interval, or statistical test is reported for this outcome in the preprint. Figure 8 shows bars without uncertainty intervals or numerical labels. The separate Online Supplement was not read.
diversity_detail.notes: Higher similarity means greater homogeneity and less diversity; reverse the sign for a diversity-oriented effect. PDF p. 33 cites Figure S6 in the separate Online Supplement for robustness across other models and temperatures.

outcomes.question: none

contrasts.reported: Table 6, TV (total vocabulary). Groenendyk: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 1859, Gemini 1.5 2131, GPT-4o mini 2690, Human 462. Graham: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 1061, Gemini 1.5 1487, GPT-4o mini 1802, Human 1146. JSD: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 1522, Gemini 1.5 2358, GPT-4o mini 2527, Human 915. Mean words (MW): Human 9.7 / 31.7 / 16.1 vs LLMs 99.0 to 215.8. Direction is mixed because Claude 3.5 Sonnet on Graham (1061) is below Human (1146); the paper says LLM answers 'generally have larger vocabularies'. No tests.

outcomes.question: none

contrasts.treatment_arm: LLM-generated answers (GPT-4o mini, Gemini 1.5, Claude 3.5 Sonnet)
contrasts.control_arm: Human-written TESS answers (JSD and Graham questions)
contrasts.reported: Figure only (Figure 7, distributions). Text: AI responses 'cluster more tightly around a lower cosine similarity to the vermin and moral disgust vectors than do human responses'; 'Whereas human responses reflect a wide range of perspectives and language use, AI responses tend to be more uniform.' No numbers or tests printed.

eligibility.reason: No one is assigned to AI help. Part I is a self-report survey of LLM use (no scored output). Part II compares answers that LLMs generated from participants' prompts with pre-ChatGPT human answers, so it is AI output versus human output, with a homogeneity outcome (pairwise tf-idf cosine similarity). The authors state they 'do not examine actual AI-assisted survey answers' (PDF p. 35 (34)). The task is open-ended opinion survey answers, not a creative task, but the cross-writer similarity outcome fits the scope's homogenization strand.

one_line_finding: In a Prolific survey (N = 794; Table 1, PDF p. 12), 34 percent report using LLMs at least sometimes for open-ended survey answers (PDF p. 4), and LLM answers generated from those users' prompts have higher average pairwise tf-idf cosine similarity than matched pre-ChatGPT human answers on all three TESS questions (Figure 8, PDF p. 33, figure only), despite being longer with generally larger vocabularies (Table 6, PDF p. 26).
